messages.mes:
The road took him with the morning traffic—carts of turnips, a drover's sheep pressed to the verge, two women in wool cloaks talking about a roof that leaked. Nobody looked twice at a young man with a staff walking toward the gates; half the city looked like that.

The walls of Glassmere rose grey and patched against the east-facing light, older than any single gatehouse. A guard at the arch glanced at his staff, then past him at the cart behind.

"Move along, keep left," the guard said, in the tone of a man who had said it forty times already that morning. "No riding in the arch."

Inside, the city woke around him. Bakers' shutters stood open, warm bread-smell fighting with the dung-and-straw of the cart lane. A boy swept a step. Somewhere a hammer rang iron in slow beats. A painted board on a corner house advertised enchantments—warding, mending, "honest rates"—beside a locksmith's plain iron sign, and neither drew a second glance from anyone passing.

He asked his way once, at a stall where a woman sold apples and dried fish, and she pointed with her chin. "Guild? Down this lane, cross the well square, big timber door with the crossed swords over it. Can't miss it."

The lane bent, the well square opened out—women filling pails, a dog drinking from the overflow—and there it stood: a broad stone hall, two stories, its timber door scarred by years of boots and gear. Above the lintel hung the crossed-swords sign, freshly painted over older paint. From inside came the low murmur of voices, the clink of a cup on wood, and someone laughing.

The door stood open. Warm lamplight and the smell of ink and old ale came out to meet the morning.

The hall was quieter inside than the laughter outside had promised. Morning light fell through high windows onto a notice board thick with pinned slips, a long table where two men studied a map over cups, and a counter of dark oak running along the far wall. Behind it sat a woman in her forties with grey coming into her dark braid, a quill behind one ear and an open ledger before her. She finished the line she was writing before she looked up.

"Morning," she said. Her voice had the flat patience of someone who said the same things all day. "Alaric Red, was it. Registering as a new member."

She pulled a blank form toward her and squared it on the counter.

"Two things you'll want to know before you sign anything. The fee is two silver, once, and it's yours paid for life—one branch is every branch, the rolls are shared. You'd start at Novice rank. That's the Guild's standing, mind, not what you can do." She tapped the ledger with the quill's feather end. "Your strength is a separate measure. There's a stone at the counter that reads your rank—that's yours already, whatever it says, Guild can't grant it or take it. The Guild rank only opens which contracts you're allowed to take."

She inked the quill and waited, elbow on the desk.

"Two silver, and your name in the book, and you're a member. Paying now?"

messages.mes:
Two silver coins crossed the oak, and she swept them into a drawer without counting what she had counted a thousand times. The quill scratched: name, date, branch. She slid the form aside and reached under the counter.

"Right. Rank stone now—hand flat on this, don't mind the tingle."

The stone set into the counter's end was the size of a loaf, worn smooth where countless palms had rested. When Alaric laid his hand on it, a faint warmth climbed his fingers and pale light stirred inside the crystal, settling into a slow glow no brighter than a candle. The clerk read it without leaning in.

"F-rank. That's where nearly everyone starts," she said. "Stone doesn't lie and it doesn't flatter. It'll read different as you grow—some do, most don't, no shame in either. Guild rank's the thing you work on."

She set a small metal plate on the counter between them: dull tin, stamped with the crossed swords and a fresh number.

"Your Guild plate. Don't lose it—replacing it costs you, and it's how any branch in the world knows who you are. Novice rank starts you on the Novice board." She tilted her head toward the notice board by the wall, thick with pinned slips. "Pick what you like off that row, bring it to me or whoever's at the desk, and we make it active before you set a foot out. Contract's only live once the desk takes it—anything else is just you and a stranger's word."

She pulled the quill from behind her ear and tapped it once against the ledger.

"That's you registered, Alaric Red. Three silver left of your five, so spend it wiser than most do their first week. Board's over there whenever you want it."

messages.mes:
The Guild hall gave him up to a street already smelling of the woolyards, and the north gate let him out onto a cart road that kept company with the stream. Carts came the other way early—wool, then tanned hides, then empty—and after the first mile the road belonged to crows and the water.

The stream ran north the way the clerk had said, and the land climbed with it. Fields gave out to rough pasture, pasture to gorse and grey stone. By midmorning the road had thinned to a track, hard underfoot, and the sound of the water changed: not the chatter of a shallow stream but something deeper, steadier, as if it had grown a body somewhere ahead.

The track bent around a shoulder of hill, and there was the cleft.

A split in the rock face, maybe thirty feet from floor to the lip of it, and the stream slid out of the dark at its base, wide and clear and cold enough that the air a spear-length from the opening carried a chill. The stone around the mouth glittered where the light caught it—not wet, but crystalline, veins of it running back into the shadow.

A post had been driven into the turf a few paces from the entrance, with a weathered board nailed to it: the paint faded but legible—GLIMMERDEEP GROTTO, and beneath it a smaller line in a clerk's careful hand: OUTER GALLERIES OPEN TO REGISTERED ADVENTURERS. THE ACADEMY THANKS YOU FOR MINDING THE MARKED STONES. White-painted boundary stones were visible just inside the mouth, a line of them curving away into the dark.

Old boot prints stitched the mud by the entrance, days old at least. Nothing fresh.

From the opening came the sound of the water and, under it, a faint chitinous click, somewhere back in the galleries—small, unhurried, the sound of something feeding.

messages.mes:
The chill took him at the mouth of the cleft and did not let go. Past the boundary stones the light failed fast, but not entirely: the crystal veins in the walls carried a pale glimmer of their own, enough to walk by, enough to see the stream slide away into a channel on the left and the path keep on along the dry stone beside it. The floor was smooth in places, worn by water and old boots both. Somewhere behind him the clicking stopped, then started again, farther off.

The passage bent twice. The second bend opened into a gallery.

It was a wide chamber, ceiling lost in glimmering dark, and the walls of it were crystal from floor to what he could see—frost-colored, faintly blue where the light touched, throwing back his own shape in broken pieces. The air tasted faintly sweet, like the smell of a struck flint.

Four beetles grazed among the crystal outcrops at its center.

They were the size of mastiffs, bodies faceted and translucent like the stone they fed on, legs ticking softly against rock as they worked at a vein of crystal with mouthparts that ground it to glittering dust. None of them had noticed the shape standing at the gallery's mouth. The nearest was two long strides from him; the others spread out across the chamber, heads down, feeding.

One of them shifted, clicked its mandibles, and kept eating.

The gallery held no other way out that he could see from here—only the crystal, the feeding beetles, and the dark at the far end where the passage presumably went on.

messages.mes:
The road south was hot by the time the sun climbed past midmorning. Dust came up off the packed earth and settled on his boots, and the hedgerows gave way to ditches, the ditches to field walls, and then the fields to the first outlying houses of Glassmere with their laundry lines and goat pens. Carters nodded to him on the way in. A dog trotted beside him for a hundred paces, decided he was boring, and went back to its own business.

Noon had the streets busy: a woman beating a rug from an upper window, the smell of onions and fat from a cookhouse doorway, two boys chasing a hoop between the wheelwright's yard and the gutter. He crossed the market square with its canvas awnings and noise and took the side street beyond it where the Guild hall stood with its door open to the heat, the plaque beside it showing the crossing swords.

Inside it was cooler. The same clerk was at the counter, grey coming into her braid, writing in a ledger with the concentration of someone who had done it a thousand times. She finished her line before she looked up.

"Back again. The beetle cull?" She held out her hand for the slip.

He gave it over. She touched the seal with two fingers, and the READY glow faded out of it under her hand. She made a mark in the ledger, turned the slip, and dropped it in a box behind her.

"Closed." Six copper and a half-dozen more in small change crossed the counter into his hand, sixty copper counted out plain. "That's the cull paid. First contract done the day after registration—some people take a week to get that far." She was already reaching for her ledger again, not unkindly. "Board's got fresh work on it if you want a look. Or don't. Your day's your own."

The hall was quiet around them: a couple of tables, somebody's abandoned mug, the board on the far wall with its papers stirring in the draft from the door.

Two adventurers came in around midday, muddy to the thigh, took a paper off the board, argued quietly about whether it was worth the walk, and went back out. A boy swept the floor and did it badly. Sunlight moved across the boards in a slow yellow band, climbed the far wall, thinned, and went the color of old honey. Somewhere outside a bell counted the hour, and then counted it again, and again.

His body mended the way a fire settles rather than leaps: the ache of the morning's climb easing out of his shoulders, mana running back down channels that had gone dry, a slow cool refilling that left him clear-headed and rested long before the last hour was done. By early evening the hall had emptied. Lamps were lit at the counter, and the clerk worked by them with the ledger's pages gone gold in the lamplight. The board's papers hung still in the dead air. Through the open door the street had gone to lamplight and long shadows, cartwheels rattling somewhere toward the market square, the smell of woodsmoke and evening cooking drifting in.

He was rested, unhurt, and the whole evening lay ahead of him in a town that was just waking to its supper hour.
